entries.title: Tigers 9, Nationals 2: Game Recap
entries.summary: The teams continue their three-game series Tuesday.
entries.content:
By Dave Hogg

DETROIT — River Ryan was outstanding in his Detroit debut and the Tigers hit three home runs to rout the Washington Nationals 9-2 on Monday night, one day after being eliminated from the American League playoff race.

Ryan, acquired from the Los Angeles Dodgers in the Tarik Skubal trade, pitched three scoreless innings. He allowed two hits and a walk with two strikeouts. Ryan is expected to start again in the season finale Sunday — the day after Justin Verlander is scheduled to make his final major league start.

Keider Montero (10-9) pitched four scoreless innings in relief of Ryan.

Washington starter DJ Herz (0-1) made his first big league appearance in nearly two years. Herz, who had Tommy John surgery in April 2025, pitched four innings, allowing four runs on five hits and two walks while striking out four.

The Tigers took a 2-0 lead in the first. Gleyber Torres walked, went to second on a wild pitch and scored on a ground-rule double from Hao-Yu Lee. After Herz got the first out, Eduardo Valencia singled to left field, with Lee scoring when James Wood misplayed the ball for an error.

Javier Báez made it 4-0 in the fourth, hitting his third homer of the season over the Tigers bullpen in left to bring home Dillon Dingler.

Detroit added five more runs in the fifth, three on Ben Malgeri's fourth homer and two on Spencer Torkelson's 25th.

That made it 9-0, but Yohandy Morales hit a two-run homer to get the Nationals on the scoreboard in the eighth.

The Tigers announced before the game that, due to a bank merger, Comerica Park will be known as Fifth Third Park starting in 2027. That's the same name as the stadium for the Toledo Mud Hens, Detroit's Triple-A team.

The teams continue their three-game series Tuesday, with Detroit RHP Drew Anderson (5-6, 3.62 ERA) facing LHP Jackson Kent (1-4, 6.40).

entries.title: Secret Service Outsources Its Polygraph Screenings for the First Time
entries.summary: The agency that protects the president and high-profile politicians says exams for new hires will be as rigorous as those from the famously tough in-house team.
entries.content:
The Secret Service’s polygraph examinations are some of the toughest in law enforcement. Job candidates spend hours getting grilled by seasoned agents who probe into their personal lives to find out if they’re fit to protect the president and the country’s highest officeholders and candidates.

For decades, that work was performed by an in-house team of specialized examiners.

Now, a push to hire thousands of new agents and officers in time for the 2028 election cycle has prompted the Secret Service to outsource some of these notoriously rigorous tests for the first time in its history.

The Secret Service and the General Services Administration this year signed contracts of up to $20 million allowing three private polygraph companies to administer the exams over the next five years.

The contractors have polygraphed hundreds of candidates across several hiring events in recent months, charging more than $2,000 per exam, according to federal contracting records and people familiar with the process.

The change comes amid a historic rise in threats against public officials as well as wider concerns about vetting standards at other federal law enforcement agencies looking to expand their ranks with an infusion of funding from Congress.

To boost recruitment, the FBI and Immigration and Customs Enforcement have lowered hiring standards and abbreviated training, eliciting concern from policymakers and current and former law enforcement officials. Secret Service leaders are under pressure to speed up hiring as well, but they have said repeatedly that they are not reducing their standards.

Secret Service Deputy Director Matthew Quinn, who authorized the contractor arrangement, said it was just as intensive as the in-house team’s and was necessary to reduce a backlog of polygraphs that had built up as the agency embarked on an aggressive recruitment campaign.

The Secret Service’s polygraph program — which typically employs roughly three dozen examiners — historically could keep pace with the churn of applicants.

But the agency turbocharged its hiring last year with the goal of netting 4,000 new employees, in preparation for a breakneck protective schedule in 2028. That led to a surge of new candidates who needed screening, according to Quinn.

In-house examiners still do about four tests a week when they aren’t being pulled into other assignments, such as the UN General Assembly meeting this week. The contract examiners are brought in periodically for additional support at events where the Secret Service allows candidates to pack the polygraph and other screening assessments into a long weekend.

“It’s been a needed force multiplier,” Quinn said in an interview. “Without it, we would not be able to maintain our hiring tempo and keep the pipeline of applicants moving through the way we are right now.”

The proposal initially faced resistance from some inside the service who objected to the break from the agency’s longstanding norms around its polygraphs.

Over the summer, an anonymous whistleblower complaint was filed with GSA’s inspector general protesting the contracts. The Washington Sun could not independently confirm the allegations in the complaint, which was first reported by the website Antipolygraph.org.

The move to third-party polygraphs also alarmed some of the Secret Service’s retired polygraph examiners, who worried that it could jeopardize vetting standards for the people tasked with guarding the president, his family and other top leaders.

“You need people who really know the job to be a gatekeeper,” said a former longtime Secret Service polygraph examiner who spoke on the condition of anonymity. “A polygraph examiner doesn’t just do polygraphs — you do protection, you do investigations, you do all of it. You know the job top to bottom. They can craft their questions and their interview to match having actually done all those jobs before.”

According to Quinn, all but two of the 20 contract polygraph examiners the agency has used so far at its hiring events are former Secret Service examiners.

All have to go through a weeklong Secret Service training where they’re revalidated on the agency’s standards. They also have to do what are known as “check ride” tests where current Secret Service examiners evaluate their performance. At the hiring events, Secret Service quality control supervisors closely review every test they administer.

“We’re cherry-picking the ones that we want,” Quinn said. “All of these people have maintained their skills. We didn't pull people off the bench who have been out for years and decided they just want to come and do polys.”

The decision to contract out some polygraphs is especially sensitive because of the program’s elite — and imposing — reputation.

The agency’s polygraph examiners have long been a small, tight-knit group, and the bar for entry is high.

Agents spend three months training in a classroom and lab with the National Center for Credibility Assessment, a federal institution that certifies government polygraph examiners. Then they train directly with the Secret Service for several more months, watching experienced mentors conduct exams before performing dozens of their own under close scrutiny.

The applicant exams often last five hours or more, and they can be grueling. They involve two components: one covering national security issues, the other focused on the candidate’s integrity. A challenge coin given to some polygraph examiners features an image of a flaming skull with wings, along with text reading, “Let the mindgames begin” and “Justica per verum” — Latin for “Justice through truth.”

Some candidates fly through the test in a few hours with no issues. But it’s not uncommon for the exams to last at least twice that long. Some agents liken it to psychological torture.

“A hellscape,” one former agent said of the process. “One of the worst experiences of my career,” said another, who retired last year after two decades with the agency.

“It’s a very psychologically challenging test that also brings in physical challenges because of the stress,” said Don Mihalek, a retired agent who protected presidents George W. Bush and Barack Obama. “You can get ready for a physical test, you can get ready for a written test. But there is no way to get ready for a polygraph other than being a complete open book when you go into it. And that’s hard for a lot of people to do.”

Though the exams themselves generally aren’t admissible in court, they have in some instances resulted in candidates admitting to crimes and being arrested, according to several current and former agents.

And they’re not just used for job applicants. The Secret Service’s polygraph examiners are routinely tapped by other law enforcement agencies for help on criminal cases and assist in the national Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force Program in investigations involving child exploitation and abuse.

“This is a proven format that has been used by the Secret Service for decades,” said a former senior Secret Service official who was also a polygraph examiner. “If anything, it has improved over the years.”

The Secret Service’s polygraph contracts highlight an ongoing scramble within the agency to expand its workforce as quickly as possible and reduce strain on its chronically overworked agents, officers and staffers. The overall goal is to get the agency to a record 10,000 employees total by around the time the presidential campaigns are in full swing.

To help get there, the agency recently awarded a $90 million contract for a national recruitment campaign that officials hope will draw more than 40,000 applicants. Hiring bonuses can now be up to $75,000, the highest of any federal law enforcement agency.

On a Reddit page run by users who claim to be current and former Secret Service staffers, applicants trade advice on how to navigate the hiring process.

In July, the page’s moderators announced a new rule: no posts or comments about the polygraph.

“We know the poly is frustrating, stressful, & unpredictable. but please don’t research it. You are hurting yourself,” the announcement read. “All you can do is relax, tell the truth, and see where the cards fall.”

entries.title: The Washington Sun Metro: Off the Ballot
entries.content:
Good morning. This is The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for Sept. 22, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

In today’s newsletter: The future of ballot initiatives, a Tom Sietsema rec in Dupont and a new starting quarterback for the Commanders. 

Capital Weather’s Daily Digit: 5/10. Autumn's first notes are a soggy song, with our coolest weather since May. But hey, it's that old refrain that we need this rain! Read the full forecast.

THE LATEST

D.C.’s version of direct democracy may get a little more difficult to pull off.

Today, the D.C. Council is expected to cast a first vote on a bill that would add new requirements and restrictions on ballot initiatives, the proposals from normal residents and groups that are presented directly to the city’s voters.

Ballot initiatives have become a regular part of D.C.’s elections. In 2024, the city’s voters approved a ballot initiative bringing ranked-choice voting to local elections; you may remember voting that way for the first time in the June primary. Voters have also been asked to weigh in on wages for restaurant workers, legalizing possession of marijuana and whether police should enforce laws against magic mushrooms.

Some say the ballot initiatives have gone too far, oversimplifying complicated public policy issues to yes-or-no votes for residents who may not have studied up. A bill from At-Large council member Anita Bonds would extend the review process for proposed ballot initiatives, limit any initiative to a single subject, and more.

Bonds has said she’s only looking to give election officials and the public the chance to weigh in on proposed initiatives before proponents start collecting signatures to get them on the ballot. Council Chair Phil Mendelson is on her side: “An initiative is written by one person; there is not the type of debate you have in the council,” he said.

Critics of the bill say the goal is to make it almost impossible to get an initiative on the ballot. In a nine-page letter to lawmakers sent last week, former D.C. Board of Elections Chair Gary Thompson called Bonds’ bill a means to “essentially strangle voter initiatives” and subject them to “death by a thousand cuts.” He added: “There is no problem to solve. There is nothing broken.”

That will be left to the council to debate today. Regardless of the outcome, a new ballot initiative will be voted on this fall: whether D.C. should ban foie gras. And two others are in the works: one that would raise the city’s minimum wage to $25 by 2029, and another to impose a two-year freeze on rents.





FROM THE DISTRICT

DCA air traffic AP - 25308827403245 (5397x3600, AR: 1.50)
In other council news, lawmakers are also expected to vote today on a bill that would ramp up parking enforcement by letting neighborhood business groups and event organizers pay off-duty city workers to write tickets, and another that would extend the period during every year that landlords have to keep air-conditioning on for tenants. Also: a bill to create an official Washington Commanders D.C. license plate.

A new AI-powered air traffic control tool touted by the Trump administration as a way to reduce delays and manage overcrowded airspace launched at D.C.-area airports Monday, The Washington Sun’s Kendall Staton reports. The three capital region airports are the first to implement the tech ahead of a nationwide rollout. It uses AI to analyze data including weather patterns, flight paths and controller staffing levels and suggest alternative routes when airspace is crowded.

Hold the line! Waterside Drive in Northwest D.C., which was supposed to close yesterday as part of a rehabilitation project, will remain open for now, WTOP reports. During preliminary excavation work last week, crews discovered a utility line dating back to the early 1900s.

The average D.C. renter pays $2,200 less per month than the average D.C. homeowner, according to a Zillow report shared in Axios D.C.’s newsletter. Over the course of a year, that's a $26,400 difference. Cha-ching!

Tonight: The Sun’s Michael Brice-Saddler will moderate two D.C. Office of Campaign Finance debates: one for at-large council candidates and another for the mayoral race. They will be streamed live on YouTube starting at 6 p.m. Shoot him an email if you have a question you’d like asked!





FROM THE DINING ROOM

Tom Sietsema, The Sun’s food correspondent, recommends a timeless Italian restaurant in Dupont Circle.

“I have no problem telling guests we’re out of something tonight.”

That’s Luigi Diotaiuti, the chef-owner of Al Tiramisu in Dupont Circle, talking. If he can’t get, say, vongole veraci (small, sweet carpet shell clams) for his linguine alle vongole, he’d rather not serve the classic Italian dish at his blink-and-you’ll-miss-it restaurant.

I called Diotaiuti — a native of Basilicata, the mountainous region in southern Italy — to ask how Al Tiramisu made it to 30 this year, which is several lifetimes in the mercurial restaurant industry. Having dined at the cozy draw the week before, however, I pretty much knew the answer.

No matter how much time has elapsed lapsed between meals at Al Tiramisu, I always return to find the same snug bar with six stools up front, the same yellow walls throughout, complimentary house-baked focaccia the moment I settle in followed by a genial server bearing a tray of fresh fish (and knowing the menu as if he had written it himself). The kitchen, under the day-to-day watch of Thomas Ayala, delivers the same consistency. There’s a reason Diotaiuti says he can’t ever take his feathery fettuccine draped in veal ragu off the menu: It’s sublime comfort. I’m frequently torn between the catch of the day, simply grilled and sparked with lemon, and lamb chops marinated with rosemary, sage and thyme, trailed by a haze of garlic.

Those who enjoy a little privacy should ask for the semi-enclosed booth, No. 15. Star-gazers should check out whoever lands at the roomier No. 1, also known as the “presidential table,” says Diotaiuti. That’s where George Clooney and company gather when they’re in town. The owner, who’s been cooking for 50 years now, predicts the world-famous actor is going to run for president in his lifetime. Maybe something he overheard? Diotaiuti also correctly predicted he’d see the first American pope. Stay tuned!





SPORTS

Marcus Mariota AP - 26263830690572 (5391x3594, AR: 1.50)
Marcus Mariota will start the Commanders’ home opener on Sunday. In coach Dan Quinn’s Monday press conference, he provided no real update on the status of Jayden Daniels’ dislocated elbow, but said Mariota will start Washington’s Week 3 meeting with the defending champion Seahawks. The Sun’s Martenzie Johnson and Alex Schiffer report that Daniels is expected to consult specialists this week as the team maps out a timeline for his return.

After Sunday’s disaster in Dallas, the Commanders are 0-2. Johnson breaks down the good, the bad and the ugly from a 37-20 loss to the Cowboys. On the one hand, the team got strong performances out of new players like Rachaad White and Stefon Diggs. On the other hand, well, there was everything else.

What to Watch Today

MLB: Nationals at Tigers, 6:40 p.m. (MLB.TV)

WNBA: Mystics vs. Sun, 7:30 p.m. (Monumental)





Thank you for reading! If you liked this newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at metro@washsun.com.

The newsletter was produced by Jaden Amos, Michael Errigo and Nikie Johnson. Finally, yesterday’s trivia answer was C) William Howard Taft. He and John F. Kennedy are the two presidents buried at Arlington National Cemetery. A special shout-out to Bob Witeck, who answered first.

entries.title: The Washington Sun: Trump Unplugged
entries.content:
Today’s notice: Trump unplugged. A progressive group remakes itself around the AI issue. “I’m glad I’m not on the ballot, I know that,” a Republican senator tells us. Missouri’s lines are still not drawn. And: The Secret Service hires polygraph vendors. 





THE LATEST

If the president speaks and there’s no camera around, does it make a sound? At the White House yesterday, Donald Trump debuted the home’s new helipad, the construction of which he’d closely supervised. A ribbon-cutting before Marine One took off for Andrews and the president’s trip to New York was a classic Trump 2.0 moment — the president showing off one of his legacy projects on the White House lawn and talking about it. Except basically no one saw and no one could hear what he said because there was a loud helicopter running behind him and no TV mics.

Capturing the sights and sounds of moments like that is the job of the TV pool. But the outlets who make up that unit are boycotting Trump after he kicked CNN, MS NOW and Politico out of the White House. Now comes the truly weirdest part of the Trump presidency, when the president who knows the most about how to be on TV has no TV cameras around.

Our Ben T.N. Mause was at the White House yesterday to see who showed up and who was allowed in. Wid Lyman, a senior correspondent for Border Hawk News, told Ben it didn’t feel like a normal day walking into the complex, even for reporters who don’t often experience Trump’s ire.

“You know, who’s next?” Lyman said, speaking for himself and not his outlet. “There’s a little bit of that in the back of your head.” The president’s frustration with the coverage from some outlets was understandable from Lyman’s perspective. But he’s still nervous about what Trump’s ban could mean for the future.

“If you don’t have that camera front and center from a nonpartisan organization, then you’re totally beholden to whatever the White House films and puts out,” Lyman said. “Which is the ultimate fear, right?”

Speaking of: The White House launched “Trump TV” last night, a 24/7 streaming channel of clips from the president’s second term. The administration insists this is not state TV but rather “a livestream of the Administration’s greatest hits, unfiltered,” per a spokesperson. The stream of the supposedly undercovered moments began with a replay of the inauguration.

More: Venezuelan DoorDash Driver Recounts Being Shot by an ICE Officer • Some Midwest Republicans Are Calling to End the Iran War to Ease Fuel Prices • Trump and Mamdani Focus on Housing at Their New York Meetup

Open tabs:

  • GOP’s war for eyeballs (Axios)
  • He spent 11 months inside DOGE. Now he wants to set the record straight. (WaPo)
  • In Trump, Xi Sees ‘Rare Window’ to Convince Taiwan That Resistance Is Futile (WSJ)
  • Wall Street Is Growing Skeptical of the Data Center Boom (NYT)




FROM THE CAMPAIGN TRAIL


First on The Sun: Working Families Party pivots to AI resistance. The progressive party is reorienting itself around the rapidly growing skepticism of artificial intelligence, our Alex Roarty reports first today. “We believe that if we’re in a moment for a political realignment, the issue of AI tech might be able to open up that realignment for us,” said Maurice Mitchell, WFP’s national director. What the WFP wants: a “pause” on AI development and a federal program to help with AI-related job losses. The group said it will use AI policy stances to determine which candidates it supports moving forward.

Republicans come to grips with economic reality: “I’m glad I’m not on the ballot, I know that,” Sen. Kevin Cramer (R-North Dakota) told The Washington Sun’s Al Weaver amid the steady stream of rising gas prices, interest rates and stubborn inflation. “It’s hard to convince people the economy’s doing great when theirs isn’t.” Al finds Republican lawmakers, including those on the ballot, have been getting an earful back home from constituents frustrated by rising household costs.

Trump policies are not helping, said Sen. Mike Rounds of South Dakota (who is, to be fair, not at risk of losing). He said ranchers reeling from White House moves to slash import tariffs sound “like a relative punched them in the gut.”

FROM THE HILL


Republican senator seeks Don Jr. subpoena: Last week, Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) said of Donald Trump Jr.’s wedding party benefactor, “It just stinks. It’s corruption, I don’t like it.” This week, he’s asking the Judiciary Committee to subpoena the president’s son to ask “legitimate questions about foreign access to members of a sitting president’s family,” according to a letter he sent to the committee’s chair and ranking member, Sens. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) and Dick Durbin (D-Illinois). Curtis also wants Hunter Biden called in as part of an overall “investigation into the use of presidential family relationships for private financial benefit.”

FROM THE REDISTRICTING WARS


Missouri keeps going: A federal appeals court ruling in favor of the state’s Republican-drawn U.S. House map possibly means yet another Supreme Court moment for Missouri, The Sun’s Manuela Silva and Kadia Goba report. News is moving so fast here that Kadia was the one to tell Rep. Emanuel Cleaver, the Democrat whose Kansas City-area district is due to be eliminated if the map goes through, about the court ruling. “This sounds so crazy because the ballots have already been printed. Some people have voted,” he said.





NEW ON THE WASHINGTON SUN

Secret Service turns to vendors for hiring screening: Secret Service leaders are under pressure to speed up hiring, but have publicly recoiled from moves to lower recruitment standards like at the FBI and other federal law-enforcement agencies, The Sun’s Derek Hakwins reports. That’s led the agency to try to find other ways to bring in new agents more quickly, like contracts to outsource recruit polygraph testing for the first time ever.

The contractors have polygraphed hundreds of candidates across several hiring events in recent months, charging more than $2,000 per exam. The USSS deputy director, Matthew Quinn, says the contractors are up to agency standards and called the arrangement “a needed force multiplier.” Derek reports that the move has caused some alarm in the tight-knit community of USSS polygraph examiners, seen by many as among the elites of the business.



More: She Received a New D.C. Medical ID. It Sent Her to an Adult Website. • Flights Resume After Massive Disruption From a Severed Telecom Cable • Federal Reserve Official Says Fighting Inflation Likely to Be ‘Painful’





NOT US

  • A populist revival in Iowa, by Peter Slevin for The New Yorker
  • ICE is targeting Haitians with new intensity. Now some are fleeing the United States for Canada. By Nick Miroff for The Atlantic
  • Bill Pulte Scrutinized Mortgages of Trump’s Political Rivals—and Todd Blanche, by Sadie Gurman and Josh Dawsey for The Wall Street Journal




Thank you for reading! If you liked this edition of The Washington Sun Newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If this newsletter was shared with you, please sign up — it’s free! Have a tip? Email us at tips@washsun.com. And as always, we’d love to hear your thoughts at newsletters@washsun.com.

The newsletter was produced by Thomas Burr and Andrew Burton.

entries.title: Republican Senators Struggle With Affordability: 'I Think I'd Talk About Other Things'
entries.summary: “I’m glad I’m not on the ballot,” said Sen. Kevin Cramer. “It’s hard to convince people the economy’s doing great when theirs isn’t.”
entries.content:
Senate Republicans’ troubles on affordability went from bad to worse after the Federal Reserve voted to raise interest rates last week, a move that will likely increase prices on a number of fronts.

The party has been on the back foot heading into the midterms due to a steady stream of negative economic news recently, the chief one being gas prices that sit close to $4.50 per gallon on average — nearly the high point since the Iran war erupted in February. Diesel prices are also hitting an all-time high. And mortgage rates are also close to eclipsing 7% once again.

The Fed’s action boosted interest rates by 25 basis points, a move that lawmakers hope quells inflation, which has been north of 3% ever since the war broke out.

But it’s the latest factor leaving Republicans at a loss as to how they should handle the issue before the November midterms.

“It’s really clumsy. I’m glad I’m not on the ballot, I know that. It’s hard to convince people the economy’s doing great when theirs isn’t,” Sen. Kevin Cramer (R-North Dakota) told The Washington Sun.

While the Fed’s move was telegraphed ahead of time, the development is expected to affect borrowers’ concerning mortgage rates, car loans and credit card interest, dealing a blow to the majority party and exacerbating members’ issues over the next six weeks.

Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas), who lost his primary to state Attorney General Ken Paxton in May, conceded that a positive Republican economic message is not easy to come by.

“I think I’d talk about different things,” Cornyn said, adding that the interest rate increase is “bad timing” for the party.

Multiple Senate Republicans noted to The Sun that they got an earful from constituents about prices over the recent summer recess, especially at the pump.

“Unless you’re an oil man in western North Dakota, you’re not really keen on high oil prices,” Cramer said.

Democrats need to flip four seats to retake the majority from Republicans, who have found themselves having to compete in contests in traditionally red states like Kansas, Alaska and Ohio because of growing dissatisfaction over rising costs.

Ever since last summer, Republican leaders have been urging members to push their economic message, headlined by what they consider popular portions of the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act. That includes making many of the 2018 tax cuts permanent, as well as no taxes on tips and overtime for some.

The U.S. war against Iran has changed that though, with consumers more focused on the immediate strain they are feeling in household budgets.

Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) noted that it is hard to find gas lower than $5 per gallon around Anchorage, with the far-flung parts of her state paying far more. She recalled a recent conversation she had with a friend in Dillingham, a commercial fishing town along Bristol Bay, who said they are paying $12.99 per gallon to fill tanks in their boats.

“And it went down. It was $13.99,” she said.

Another factor hurting Republicans is Trump’s decision to pause tariffs on 300,000 metric tons of imported beef in the face of sky-high prices.

Ag-state members made their feelings known, saying that it is a mistake as it will hurt the bottom lines of ranchers, a key constituency, who have already been struggling.

When asked what he’s heard from voters back home, Sen. Mike Rounds (R-South Dakota), who is up for reelection, said that slashing the beef import tariff was, in their minds, like being “hurt by a relative.”

“It’s like a relative punched them in the gut,” Rounds told The Sun.

Making matters worse, there’s nothing the Senate can do before members leave later this month until after the election that will make an impact. The chamber is currently working to pass a bill to overhaul college sports after Senate Majority Leader John Thune promised Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) that he would take it up after the Clarity Act.

Some in the party wish they were doing more to combat voters’ economic concerns. Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), a key incumbent up for reelection in November, namechecked permitting reform as one item, among others, where “we would demonstrate that we understand the concerns of American families.”

Lawmakers in both parties have been pushing to strike a deal to streamline rules on new infrastructure and energy projects, but that’s hardly considered a sure thing. The House is also out until after the midterms, meaning that the earliest anything could pass both chambers is November.

Murkowski also argued that permitting reform was the one realistic thing that would help both on the costs front and politically.

“It would help [Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska)]. It would help everyone who is up. It would help everyone who is not up,” Murkowski told reporters, adding that gas prices in her state are unsustainable.

“People are feeling it, and they don’t like it. They don’t like it at all,” Murkowski continued. “And what kind of response are we seeing out of the White House? Is there a recognition that there’s a connection here? If there is, I’m not hearing anybody enunciate it.”

entries.title: How the D.C. Government Wants to Use AI
entries.summary: Leaders say AI could assist the workers who keep D.C. running. But concerns over job displacement and privacy remain.
entries.content:
Overgrown grass. Trash strewn everywhere. D.C.’s Department of Buildings is constantly fielding complaints about the District’s thousands of vacant properties.

Each time someone complains, DOB discharges an inspector to take a look, something it’s done more than 11,400 times this past fiscal year alone. That’s in addition to thousands more inspections focused on poor conditions in occupied housing or external property maintenance at private, owner-occupied property.

“It puts us in a space where the public controls the amount of work we’re doing,” said Keith Parsons, DOB’s director of strategic enforcement. “[Complaints are] still super valuable and super helpful, but we do want to take ownership … and take some of the burden off of citizens.”

To become more proactive, DOB is one of many D.C. agencies considering using artificial intelligence. Specifically, it’s looking to contract a company that can take street photographs of property exteriors and use AI to determine where there may be housing code violations that need abatement. A lot of vacant properties look vacant to a car going by, Parsons noted.

“We want AI to save us work,” he said. “It’s supposed to be helping us be more efficient.”

That is the approach being taken by administrators at many of the city’s agencies, in conjunction with a broad framework laid out by Mayor Muriel Bowser, that experts say could allow the District to become a leading city in implementing AI — helping it to stretch limited resources, automate tedious paperwork and generally speed up city services.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

But given the speed with which the technology is evolving, some observers are noting potential concerns with adopting AI for city use — including the possibility of the technology displacing jobs currently performed by humans and the privacy concerns it could present for residents.

“We’ve been talking about the Mayor’s order on AI and making sure we move forward in conjunction with those values,” Parsons said.

In February 2024, Bowser signed an executive order that established ground rules for how District agencies adopt AI. The order detailed six core values — including privacy, equity and human accountability — that agencies must weigh before deploying AI tools. It also created a citywide AI task force and set a timeline requiring every D.C. agency to submit a formal strategic plan by October 2026, while giving the Office of the Chief Technology Officer broad authority to vet and approve new technology before deployment.

“What the mayor wants is really for the city itself to have that understanding and that awareness of how the technology is being utilized,” said Chris Rodriguez, the assistant city administrator whose office reviews any agency plans for using AI. “This is a new technology. This is something that a lot of cities are utilizing, and we wanted to make sure that there's a governance structure in place to be able to implement it.”
Muriel Bowser (5359x3572, AR: 1.50)The order makes D.C. an early leader on AI among cities, said Christopher Jordan, a program manager of AI and innovation at the National League of Cities. The District, he said, is one of the only cities nationwide to have mandated AI training for city employees and was early to issue guidelines.

While city agencies’ annual performance oversight filings to the D.C. Council aren’t exhaustive, they help illustrate how they are putting those guidelines into practice — or at least, how they’re preparing to.

‘We Don’t Expect AI to Answer a 911 Call’

Public safety and emergency response agencies are among those taking the most active steps.

D.C.’s Metropolitan Police Department secured conditional approval for an intelligence platform that pulls together video feeds and license plate readers into a real-time hub. In line with the mayor’s order, MPD noted that AI-generated data is not used when officers conduct stops, searches or arrests, or while making use-of-force decisions.

Meanwhile, officials with the Office of Unified Communications — which manages D.C.’s 311 and 911 systems — say they are working on projects to route automated calls through an AI chatbot to generate dispatch events.

“The goal is to get the AI to answer the more routine service request and the calltaker is focused on the more complex ones,” said Gavin Suares, OUC’s chief information officer, adding that AI is being tested more extensively on 311 calls.

For 911 calls, AI has only been used for quality assurance checks. But Suares says the technology could have additional uses. “We don’t expect AI to answer a 911 call, but there are use cases: quality assurance, translation and transcription,” he said.

Oversight filings show that behind the scenes, some of D.C.’s operational and social services departments are turning to AI to tackle chronic efficiency challenges. The Department of Public Works plans to incorporate an AI-enabled waste sorting system into its overhauled Benning Road transfer station. The Department of Human Services said in oversight filings that officials are exploring AI upgrades to help fix the city’s SNAP benefit payment accuracy rate — an area in which D.C. lags behind, per federal data.

Officials from the city’s Board of Ethics and Government Accountability suggested to the council that AI-powered software could be useful for agencies bogged down by heavy public records backlogs.

The District is also experimenting with integrating AI into routine aspects of local governance, having launched a free regional AI marketplace for job seekers and piloted a university-developed AI platform to facilitate large-scale policy discussions with residents.

Rodriguez says D.C. will be the second jurisdiction in the nation to use a government-specific version of Claude, the AI tool developed by Anthropic.

‘Nobody Can or Should Relax Here’

The District is well positioned to become a leader in AI adoption, Mark Muro, a senior fellow at Brookings Metro, told The Washington Sun. The area is home to hundreds of AI startups and a well educated talent pool, and many companies are already implementing AI in their work.

But D.C. — which already has the highest unemployment rate in the country — will need to balance the economic opportunity AI could bring to its agencies with the potential for job displacement, Muro said.

“We haven’t really seen massive disruption yet, but that’s a question,” Muro said of AI-induced layoffs. “Nobody can or should relax here.”

Rodriguez stresses that he doesn’t see AI substituting for the work currently done by city workers. “It's meant to assist,” he said. “It's not meant to replace.”

The Department of Buildings wants to reduce the number of manned inspections of vacant property — one AI-assisted survey would do the work of 100,000 manned inspections — but the idea is to refocus those human workers on other areas like inspections of occupied property or illegal construction, Parsons said. And Suares noted that AI’s quality assurance checks on 311 and 911 calls would take 50 or 60 new human employees to handle.

But the widespread adoption of AI in city government raises privacy concerns. That’s especially the case in D.C. Public Schools, which has quietly rolled out AI tools for staff and students — including from Microsoft, one of its principal technology vendors. Some parents say they were never notified about the use of AI for kids, and are unclear what safeguards will be employed.

“One of the top concerns many parents have is how is our kids’ data being used? What accounts are being set up with very little parental notification or consent?” said Maya Mechenbier, a DCPS parent and leader of Schools Beyond Screens D.C. “Is there evidence for their use in schools? If there is a new platform that is supposed to help with kids’ reading, has that product been independently tested relative to a human approach?”

Earlier this month DCPS unveiled new guidelines on the use of technology in classrooms, and Mechenbier says school officials are now sharing lists of approved tools — including AI — and those still under consideration.

As for residents who don’t like the idea of having their homes photographed and run through AI programs, DOB points out that the agency does have jurisdiction over the exteriors of all private property in the District. What’s more, vehicles have long captured street view images of people and their homes, Parsons pointed out.

Still, concerns linger. Rep. James Comer (R-Kentucky) wrote in a letter to DOB he was worried about the initiative’s potential to “ensnare” property owners with excessive fees, “putting them on a path towards foreclosure.”

Another worry is that AI could target, and aggressively fine, those living in low-income communities. But Gavin Baum-Blake, the CEO of City Detect, a company that performs AI-assisted property inspections nationwide, said he ensures his software centers equity.

“It doesn't look for beauty, it looks for things that are out of code,” he said. “A house that's worth $70,000 that doesn't have any issues is going to be rated the exact same as a $3 million house without any issues. That's all that it's looking for.”

D.C. residents have expressed excitement around improving public services and communication from the city, said Jordan, who also serves as a public member of D.C.’s Advisory Group on AI Values Alignment. But residents have certainly had questions, particularly about how AI will be deployed in schools, he said.

“Overall, I think there is a cautious optimism,” Jordan said. “When the public can see inside the city's strategy and their intent, I think that it just creates a much better forum to have these conversations, rather than starting with distrust.”
entries.author: Zara Norman, Martin Austermuhle, Michael Brice-Saddler

entries.title: Lessons From the Final Days of the Nationals’ Season
entries.summary: A customized bobblehead, pitchers showing promise, and a star player benched before owning his mistake.
entries.content:
ST. LOUIS — Late Sunday afternoon at Busch Stadium, reporters gathered by Erik Tolman’s locker for the wrong reasons. He had, just a bit ago, given up a one-run lead in the eighth on a solo homer to Ivan Herrera. That was the start of turning a near-win into a 5-3 loss to the Cardinals, keeping the Nationals from a sweep. It was the Nationals’ 42nd blown save of the season, an MLB record and counting.

The Nats (73-84) have still won six of their past nine games. But because they didn’t win Sunday, Tolman talked for a few minutes about failure. About learning from it. About not dwelling on mistakes for too long. Once he was finished, he packed his things for the flight to Detroit, where the Nationals are playing this week before ending their season with a home series against the Mets. Tolman grabbed his headphones. He took a sip of a light brown smoothie. And then he reached to the top shelf of his locker, which was where he had put his Erik Tolman bobblehead.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

Yes, an Erik Tolman bobblehead. The only one in the world. After he debuted in late August, a Midwesterner named Chris contacted him on social media, asking Tolman if he would like his very own bobblehead. Chris lives about two hours from St. Louis. If Tolman were into it, he offered to bring it to the Nats-Cardinals games this past Friday. Chris just asked for some gear in return, which wound up being a pair of Tolman’s cleats. The bobblehead depicts Tolman, a lefty reliever, mid-delivery. On the base, it has the date of first big league appearance: 8-22-26.

“I’ve never had anything customized like that,” Tolman, 27, told me Sunday morning. “I mean, look, that’s pretty damn cool.”

He’s certainly gained fans inside the organization, too. At Busch Stadium over the weekend, I asked a handful of people for their most immediately intriguing arms in the Nats’ bullpen, trying to figure out who might grow the fastest into high-leverage roles. The most common answers were Tolman and Orlando Ribalta, a hard-throwing righty who’s on the injured list with right forearm inflammation. Both were acquired by the previous front office, Tolman as a 14th-round pick in 2021, Ribalta as a 12th-round pick in 2019. And that means both are in the process of proving themselves to the new front office, which will be making a lot of roster decisions in the near future.

Some players have had months to do that. Tolman is making use of his five weeks. He didn’t allow a run until his sixth appearance. His more recent outings have not been as clean. On Sunday, he gave up that game-tying homer. On Saturday, asked to hold a ninth-inning lead against the Cardinals, he was hurt by bad luck when a soft grounder — hit by Nathan Church, his high school teammate — bounced off second base and turned into a leadoff double.

In 12 ⅓ innings, Tolman has recorded three saves and 12 strikeouts, and has allowed five earned runs.The bobblehead, then, will always be one reminder that he was here, that he pitched at Busch Stadium, Nationals Park and a handful of other big league fields. But just getting there was never the goal. In 2023, a freak injury almost led to the amputation of his right foot, which happened right after he had recovered from two elbow surgeries. He thinks a lot about the long road back, which included doubts about whether he would ever walk normally again, let alone pitch in the major leagues. There’s also a constant reminder on his right leg: a black brace he wears for all physical activity.

“I didn’t come this far to be average,” Tolman said. “It’s really as simple as that.”

Josiah Gray can relate. Gray made his season debut in St. Louis on Friday night, two years and two weeks after he last pitched in the majors. In that time, he also battled elbow injuries, the slow drip of multiple rehabs, those similar doubts about whether he could ever be the same. Five Septembers ago, he was central to the Nats’ plans, having just arrived as a key piece for the return for Max Scherzer and Trea Turner. Now, though, his future with the organization is much more complicated. As an arbitration-eligible player, Gray could be non-tendered — or, in plainer terms, cut loose — early in the offseason to make room for younger talent on the 40-man roster.

In the meantime, all he can do is maximize whatever chances he gets in this final week of the season. In that long-awaited appearance Friday, Gray pitched the ninth inning, a change from his usual starter role. He gave up a leadoff single, then retired the next three batters to finish a 9-1 win. He smacked his chest twice, looked at the sky and smacked his chest again. His fastball touched 94 mph. The next day, when someone complimented him on that in the dugout, Gray said, “It’s amazing what happens when your elbow doesn’t hurt.”

DJ Herz, the Nationals’ starter in Detroit on Monday, also missed close to two years with arm issues before making his season debut against the Tigers. In a 9-2 loss, Herz pitched four innings and allowed four runs on five hits, two walks and a back-breaking homer for Javier Báez. Gray then pitched a scoreless seventh and eighth. Beyond auditioning for their new coaches and front office, Herz and Gray are reintroducing themselves to a fan base that once viewed them as small bursts of hope.

“Obviously 2026 isn’t 2021,” Gray said on Friday afternoon. “But at the end of the day, this next week and a half, hit the ground running and see where they see me slotted in with the future of this thing.”

Keibert Ruiz can relate to the difference five years makes. Like Gray, he came to Washington in the Scherzer-Turner trade, back when the Nats first tore down their roster to start building it back up. He was the biggest get in the deal, almost immediately tapped as the catcher of the present and future. That led to an eight-year, $50 million extension before the 2023 season. But then Ruiz struggled to find his footing. For the next three years, he posted a .656 on-base-plus-slugging percentage in 331 games, well below league average. And somehow even more concerning was his defense, as he ranked toward the bottom in advanced pitch framing stats in 2025.

This season, though, has been a total revelation. Ruiz has been an above-average framer, per Statcast, and has a .770 OPS in 101 games. A big factor has been Bobby Wilson, the Nats’ first-year major league catching coordinator. Also, at the start of the second half of the season, the team began calling some pitches from the dugout, an approach born of an almost unwavering commitment to using analytics for strategic decisions. But one of the exceptions to that is Ruiz, who has continued to call pitches because of the trust he’s earned from the staff.

Pitchers Cade Cavalli and Jake Irvin call their own games from the mound, as does lefty Andrew Alvarez (though not always). The strategy of calling pitches from the dugout is most prevalent with relievers and when rookie Harry Ford is behind the plate. Ruiz, 28, is proud of keeping the responsibility. He’s not, however, ready to call his season a complete success.

“What’s happened with the bullpen, that’s on me, too,” Ruiz told me, referring to all the blown saves. “There is more that I feel like I can do still.”

James Wood can relate to that last bit, which is really to say it applies to every player on the team. From the front office to the field, this is a young organization still finding itself, working through growing pains together. And on Saturday night, Wood, the Nats’ best player, was right in the middle of that. In the top of the ninth, he hit a dribbler, sprinted out of the box and then slowed down when he thought the first baseman had fielded it cleanly. But the first baseman had actually bobbled the ball, which Wood didn’t realize until it was too late.

He sped up again but was out by a good margin. Blake Butera, the club’s first-year, 34-year-old manager, pulled him from the game, an eventual 8-5 win in 11 innings. Afterward, Butera said the decision was partly to improve the Nats’ outfield defense, swapping Wood out for Jacob Young. The other part, though, was because Wood hadn’t hustled all the way down the line. This has happened a couple of times in recent weeks, so Butera chose to send a message through his star player. He told reporters: “He’s never doing it on purpose. Just sometimes it doesn’t look great, and that’s our job, to let him know that.”

Minutes later, the two of them quickly chatted in the clubhouse, Wood nodding at Butera from his swivel chair. In game 155 of 162, in the final days of another losing season, there were still lessons to learn, impressions to make, a foundation that needs attention, all the way to the end.

“I feel like we’re trying to build something here, and I plan on being here for a long time,” Wood said. “So I feel like I’ve got to be able to set an example.”

entries.title: Progressives Plan to Capitalize on the AI Backlash
entries.summary: The Working Families Party wants to pivot to focusing on AI as the technology becomes a defining issue.
entries.content:
A leading progressive group is reorienting its organizational mission to focus on combatting artificial intelligence programs and the Big Tech companies developing them. The group argues that the fight against the emergent technology will be the country’s defining political issue for the foreseeable future.

It’s a major change from the Working Families Party, a long-standing New York-based group that supports progressive candidates nationwide and is often at odds with the Democratic Party establishment. But its leaders say the change is necessary because of a lack of leadership on AI issues, including from Democrats.

“We believe it’s time for a hard pivot to make this election a referendum on these technologies,” Maurice Mitchell, WFP’s national director, said in an interview.

WFP’s announcement underscores the already-significant effect AI is having on politics, as everyone from future presidential candidates to congressional leaders scramble to stay ahead of a public with fast-changing views on the subject.

It also reflects the growing belief among progressives that the issue’s rising importance gives the political left a prime populist attack against Republicans, tapping into widespread voter anxiety over what the technology could mean for public safety and jobs.

“We believe that if we’re in a moment for a political realignment, the issue of AI tech might be able to open up that realignment for us,” Mitchell said.

Mitchell said that the WFP had heard concerns about AI all year from its local leaders and from voters, worries that he added have only intensified as experts warn of the existential risks the technology could pose.

“It’s clear that the majority of people do not trust these corporations, do not trust the people who lead these companies, are very anxious about these technologies and are looking for some leadership,” he said. “WFP is going to fill that void.”

In a memo obtained by The Washington Sun, WFP argued that companies needed to “hit pause” on AI development, citing concerns that the technology could directly harm humanity or that the entire industry is a financial bubble whose collapse could bring about catastrophe.

The group said it would support candidates who back an aggressive agenda to rein in industry and pressure other members of the party to do the same. WFP officials said they would support Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Greg Casar’s ban on artificial superintelligence, which would temporarily pause “advanced AI” development.

“It is our strong belief that combatting the unchecked power of Big Tech corporations will be a defining issue of the time, and the Working Families Party is prepared to be part of leading the opposition,” the memo said.  

President Donald Trump has been dismissive of rising concerns about the safety of AI, calling the fear “a hoax.” He’s also continued to push for the rapid construction of data centers across the country, although some Republican congressional candidates have opposed their development.

For most of this year, the proliferation of data centers across the country has been a major campaign issue, as candidates from both parties argued that their construction needed to slow down. But the overall concern about AI development intensified earlier this month, when former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon quit his job and warned about the technology’s existential threat to humanity.

“We’re going to be really tying together these concerns around this theme of the people versus the machines,” Mitchell said. “And we think there’s going to be a lot of power in that approach.”

WFP officials said they are also advocating for a federal jobs program to help with AI-related job losses and want to curb AI programs that would help determine health insurance denials or surveillance pricing.

entries.title: The Good, the Bad and the Ugly from the Commanders' Loss to Dallas
entries.summary: Jayden Daniels went down, Marcus Mariota stepped up and the secondary struggled.
entries.content:
A botched two-point-conversion attempt seems tame compared to what happened to the Commanders in Dallas on Sunday. Quarterback Jayden Daniels dislocated his elbow for the second time in less than 10 months, throwing Washington’s season into disarray after just two games. On the other side of the ball, another porous performance by the retooled defense has the Commanders searching for answers ahead of their home opener against the defending champion Seahawks in Week 3.

Here’s a closer look at Sunday’s loss to the Cowboys, with some thoughts on the game tape and coach Dan Quinn’s Monday afternoon press conference:

Daniels’ injury happened on an option play.

Washington lined up in 13 personnel (one running back, three tight ends), and Daniels was supposed to have the option to either cut in toward the goal line or toss the ball out to running back Rachaad White.

On the right side of the formation, the offensive line was overleveraged — there were four Cowboys defenders against just two blockers. Cowboys defensive end Jonathan Bullard beelined toward Daniels, who would have had a toss to White had left guard Chris Paul not stepped on his foot. Daniels threw the ball away as he fell, dislocating his elbow when he hit the ground.

Andrew Wylie got to the outside shoulder of his assignment while John Bates pushed his man in the opposite direction, potentially giving White a path to the end zone.

To that point in the game, Daniels had punished the Cowboys’ defense on the ground. His 69 yards on six scrambles was a career high for one half, according to NFL Research.

“It was certainly a freakish one of getting stepped on,” Quinn said of the injury. “Sometimes hard to explain.”

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

Marcus Mariota AP - 26264700180862 (8640x5760, AR: 1.50)
Marcus Mariota looked like a starting quarterback.

For someone who had zero expectations of taking the field on Sunday, Mariota held up surprisingly well. In one half of work, he finished 11 of 16 passes for 111 yards and a touchdown, picking up many of those yards in impressive fashion.

Mariota was fighting for his life in the pocket for most of his drop-backs. He was pressured on seven of 17, but was able to make magic happen on a few.

Late in the third quarter, Mariota stepped up in the pocket as large men Quinnen Williams and LT Overton barreled towards him. He evaded a swipe by Overton, and while getting pushed to the ground by linebacker Malachi Lawrence, threw the ball to Dyami Brown inches away from the sideline for an 18-yard gain. In the fourth quarter, facing a third-and-4, Mariota Texas two-stepped out of Donovan Ezeiruaku’s way and found White in the flat for a first down.

While the Seahawks’ pass rush has pressured at an average rate through two games, they’ve allowed the fewest yards per play (3.8). Last season, Seattle totaled five sacks and an interception in a 38-14 rout of Washington.

Quinn said Mariota’s presence won’t change much of the playbook, though it can be assumed that designed runs, like the option play where Daniels got hurt, will be rare for the 12-year veteran.

“We’re fortunate in that way, that he’s put in all the same timelines and guidelines with the players,” Quinn said of Mariota. “So it won’t be exactly the same, but fortunately they’ll have a lot of similarities.”

CeeDee Lamb made mincemeat of the Commanders’ secondary. 

Coming into the week, there was no doubting that Lamb would be a threat. Aside from having the third-most receiving yards (7,416) from 2020 to 2025, Lamb torched the Vikings last year when Commanders defensive coordinator Daronte Jones was an assistant with Minnesota.

And on Sunday, Lamb chopped up Washington’s zone defense as well. He found plenty of space on a first-quarter catch that went for 23 yards. Later in that same drive, he caught a three-yard touchdown after a breakdown between cornerback Mike Sainristil and safety Nick Cross.

https://x.com/NFL/status/2101772374253449298

Lamb feasted on man coverage as well. He made corner Rasul Douglas bite on a cut to the inside before breaking back toward the sideline for a 38-yard gain, and burned Sainristil on a go route in single coverage for a 24-yard score.

“I didn't love the communication, the attention out on the premiums with CeeDee and with George Pickens,” Quinn said Monday. “So we've got work to do on that spot.”

Lucky for the Commanders they don’t face the leading receiver in yards (277) and yards after catch (112) this week in their home opener.

Oh, wait.

Washington’s pass rush got to Dak Prescott, but it didn’t matter.

Believe it or not, but the Commanders’ pass rush fared well on Sunday. Of Prescott’s 36 drop-backs, he was pressured on 15 of them, according to NFL Research. That 41.7% rate was the 11th highest in the league in Week 2. Washington also had two sacks.

https://x.com/Commanders/status/2101786800263921811

But on those 15 pressures, Prescott still completed nine of 13 pass attempts for 101 yards.

One example: On a play in the first quarter, edge rusher Odafe Oweh got in Prescott’s face just as the quarterback launched the ball to Lamb, who was standing alone 20 yards down the field. On a third-and-8 in the third quarter, linebacker Sonny Styles charged right at Prescott, who stepped out of the way and hit a wide-open Jake Ferguson for a 14-yard gain.

Prescott was even better when Washington gave him time to cook, completing 17 of 18 passes for 178 yards and four touchdowns when not under pressure.

“Collectively, defensively, we didn't make life hard enough on Dak in those spots,” Quinn said. “So those are the things that kept me up for sure last night.”
entries.author: Martenzie Johnson

entries.title: She Received a New D.C. Medical ID. It Sent Her to an Adult Website.
entries.summary: The Department of Health Care Finance says an old web address is still printed on some materials.
entries.content:
When Kristin Wallace received a new D.C. medical identification card in the mail this week, she didn’t expect it to lead her to a scam website with adult content.

Wallace moved back to the District in July after living in Los Angeles for the past seven years. Unemployed and moving in with her mom, she figured she'd have to start from scratch to get health insurance.

When Wallace applied for Medicaid in early August, officials told her the renewal process would take roughly 45 days. So when she opened an official letter from the Department of Health Care Finance on Sunday, she hoped progress had been made.

“I’ve just been looking for any communication, because I haven’t had cards sent to me in the past, however many years I’ve been enrolled,” she said.

Wallace, who said she prefers to fill out forms online, typed in the web address printed on the back of the ID to log in to the online portal, only to be sent to a phishing website featuring a scantily clad female cartoon character instead.

“I just typed in the address that’s there, and it took me to — I’m not sure what language it was — but some Eastern European big-titty website,” Wallace said.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

After Wallace quickly exited her browser, she began calling officials listed on the ID for help. For most of them, Wallace said, it was the first time they had heard about the issue, and they couldn’t provide much assistance.

In a statement sent to The Washington Sun, DHCF apologized to residents, providers and beneficiaries for the error and said it is currently working with the Office of the Chief Technology Officer to prevent any future issues.

“No DHCF systems were compromised, and no beneficiary or provider information was exposed,” the statement read. “The incorrect domain in question is no longer used or owned by DC Government, and the URL was not correctly updated on some material.”

Officials said the correct website is medicaid.dc.gov

Wallace shared her experience on Reddit on Monday morning. The 34-year-old said she was relieved she was young enough to notice the issue, and was worried for older people who may be more susceptible to the scam.

“I’m glad that I’m a mostly competent 30-something-year-old and I don’t know how many elderly folks or folks with mental disabilities greater than mine are opening this and potentially dying because they aren’t getting healthcare,” Wallace said.
